summary.title: MinT: Managed Infrastructure for Training and Serving Millions of LLMs

details: Post-training now yields many policy variants (tenants, product branches, rollback points, eval snapshots) over a few expensive base-model deployments; treating each variant as a full checkpoint/full-model server does not scale.
Full-checkpoint (or merge-based LoRA) workflows force materializing and moving whole models across the training-serving boundary.

MinT (MindLab Toolkit): a managed, Tinker-compatible service for LoRA post-training (SFT/DPO/RL) and online serving in which the exported LoRA adapter revision is the sole managed policy unit crossing training to serving.

Key design principle: separate the executable adapter revision (frozen PEFT tensors in serving layout) from a durable service-owned policy record (base version, rank/targets, training checkpoint, rollout records, exported revisions), with base models kept resident and trainers time-slicing LoRA state over them.

Three-tier residency separation for scale-out: durable addressable adapter catalog vs. per-engine CPU adapter cache vs. GPU batch slots, with cold adapter loading treated as scheduled, admission-controlled service work.
Service plane (validate, enqueue, pollable operation ids, policy-record resolution, worker admission/eviction) separated from compute plane.
Compute roles: single-worker PEFT trainers, distributed Megatron trainer groups (TP/PP/EP), vLLM sampler/serving actors with LoRA slots.
Distributed export gathers TP LoRA slices, deduplicates shared-expert tensors, collects per-expert LoRA from EP owners into one PEFT revision.

Training-serving consistency: R3-style MoE expert-route replay (mask token when route unmappable); IcePop-style importance-weight zeroing outside a trusted ratio band for GLM-5 DSA sparse attention (no per-token DSA replay).
Dense: Qwen3-4B SFT (FinGPT/FinEval suite) and chat-DPO; Qwen3-8B-base GRPO on DAPO-AIME24, evaluated on AIME24/25/26 (temp 1.0, top-p 0.7, 32K cap, seed 42).
MoE: Qwen3-30B-A3B and Qwen3-235B-A22B GRPO on AIME24 (235B: 32 A800 GPUs, Megatron TP=4, EP=8, PP=1, plus 16-GPU TP=16 serving); Kimi K2 1.04T (32.6B active) countdown-task LoRA RL on 64 H800 GPUs.
GLM-5.1 LoRA GRPO for Macaron-A2UI generative UI: 32 prompts x 8 responses per step, 40 steps, reward stack with hard-fail notes.
LawBench AutoResearch: proxy-screen then full-benchmark confirmation of recipe/data-manifest candidates on Qwen3-4B.

Handoff probe: adapter-only load vs. merge-and-load full checkpoint, on Qwen3-4B (rank-32 LoRA, 252 MiB vs. 8.061 GB) and Qwen3-30B (rank-16, 1.692 GB vs. 61.084 GB), timing materialization/load plus rollout.
Utilization probe: 3 concurrent GRPO policies vs. sequential schedule under the same resident-base allocation, tracking wall time, GPU utilization and peak memory.
Qwen3-30B-A3B rank-1 MoE LoRA on one 4-GPU TP=4 vLLM serving actor; prompt length 1024, max output 64.
Built and audited 1,000,000 packed adapter revisions in 100 shards (256-adapter read audit); legacy 1k-100k catalog sweep retained.

Probes: repeated-hotset vs. unique-adapter cache ladders (up to 2048 targets), 64-adapter same-batch window, open-loop Poisson sweep with TTFT<=5s SLO, cold-load staircase (N=16), packed vs. fragmented tensor loading, hot reload with admission off/on and two-phase readiness.
Baselines/negative probes: native vLLM with standard PEFT 1k pool (packed layout fails to load), sticky-hash routing, adaptive activation schedulers, fleet-level active-wave sizing model.

key_findings.finding: Making the exported LoRA adapter (not a merged checkpoint) the training-serving artifact removes the dominant materialization cost of the handoff.
key_findings.evidence: Handoff step drops 18.3x on Qwen3-4B (adapter load 0.036 s vs. 71.82 s merge materialization; 252 MiB vs. 8.061 GB) and 2.85x on Qwen3-30B (46.455 s vs. 402.245 s; 1.692 GB vs. 61.084 GB), and adapter bytes are ~3.3% of the 4B bf16 base-weight floor at rank 32 (~0.10% at rank 1).

key_findings.finding: Time-slicing multiple LoRA policies over one resident base fills schedule gaps and cuts wall time without extra memory.
key_findings.evidence: Three concurrent GRPO policies finish in 1736.1 s vs. 3081.2 s sequential on Qwen3-4B (1.77x) and 7008.4 s vs. 10130.0 s on Qwen3-30B (1.45x), with peak memory unchanged (65.6 GiB and 68.0 GiB respectively).

key_findings.finding: Million-scale policy addressability is achievable as a built artifact while engine-local residency stays bounded at hundreds of cached and 64 same-batch adapters.
key_findings.evidence: 1,000,000 packed rank-1 Qwen3-30B adapters built across 100 shards with 0 errors (138,521 s, 762.2 MB/s) and a 256/256 shard-spanning read audit; serving on one TP=4 actor reaches 369 cached adapters at a 512 hotset and 550 under 2048-adapter weak locality (p95 63.14 s), with 64 distinct adapters in the tested decoding batch and 100% TTFT<=5s through 2 rps (72.1% at 4 rps).

key_findings.finding: The online bottleneck is cold adapter activation, not catalog registration, and it must be scheduled with readiness gating rather than exposed immediately.
key_findings.evidence: Registering 16 adapters takes 1.66 s total (p95 0.136 s), yet immediate first-touch raises existing warm TTFT p95 from 0.549 s to 20.84 s; admission off gives warm p95 24.03 s with 10 stalls >20 s, admission on gives 9.71 s with 0 stalls but new-adapter load p95 294.96 s, while two-phase readiness yields warm p95 9.63 s, 0 stalls, ready-path load p95 0.00 s at the cost of a 409.04 s prewarm span; adaptive higher-concurrency prewarm variants regress warm tails (cap=4: 28.63 s, 33 stalls).

key_findings.finding: MoE LoRA cold-load cost is object-bound rather than byte-bound, so packing expert tensors sharply speeds live loading.
key_findings.evidence: Packing cuts tensor objects from 37,248 (37,152 <=4 KB) to 672 with file size 110.75 MB to 105.58 MB, giving 54.8x faster tensor reads, 29.5x faster loader-object build, and 8.5-8.7x faster live engine loads (medians under 0.2 s at N=4/8/16); unique cold adapters otherwise serialize into a 1.375-23.267 s staircase (~1.35-1.40 s per policy) with small API queue wait.
